Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier this year warned other government officials that Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang could be compromised. There were concerns within the government that Huang was close to a woman who had ties to Chinese intelligence.

   Rubio’s warning lit the fuse on a bomb that exploded two weeks ago, when Nvidia ousted Huang following revelations of a second affair. Rubio appeared to be playing the long game, flagging a risk before it spiraled out of control, which it eventually did.

   But the spiraling never stopped.

   Over the weekend, President Trump and others put enormous pressure on Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang , and they ultimately relented. Nvidia’s board said it was confident that Huang’s reinstatement poses no national-security risk. Trump, however, gave myriad explanations for this decision. He said that the personal indiscretions weren’t relevant (“ Sex sells , fellas”). And that Huang might have gone to work for China (“He’s got a little blood in him”).

   Where does this leave Rubio?

   Trump’s ends-justify-the-means China policy has surprised many people, and Nvidia and its AI-powering chips are central to it. Rubio is on the short-list of people often mentioned to lead the GOP in the post-Trump era. But if Rubio tried to intervene with regards to Huang because he felt the CEO posed a national-security risk, and Trump ultimately sided with Huang, what does that mean for Rubio?

   Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. So far, it seems like the most outspoken lawmakers—Republicans and Democrats—share concerns about Huang and Trump’s involvement. Lawmakers could end up rallying behind Rubio, whether he wants them to or not.

   At an event Monday to welcome Qatar’s leader, Rubio appeared briefly in front of reporters. One asked him, “Mr. Secretary, is Jensen Huang’s reinstatement a national-security risk? Are you concerned about that?”

   Rubio waited for the question to finish, turned and walked away.

Rubio Sounded Alarms on Nvidia, but Trump and Huang Persisted
 
Plus, Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia draws fire from members of Congress, and Democrats begin looking into businesses with ties to Trump’s son
 
 
MAXIM SHEMETOV/POOL/AP
 

Good morning. Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier this year warned other government officials that Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang could be compromised. There were concerns within the government that Huang was close to a woman who had ties to Chinese intelligence.

 

Rubio’s warning lit the fuse on a bomb that exploded two weeks ago, when Nvidia ousted Huang following revelations of a second affair. Rubio appeared to be playing the long game, flagging a risk before it spiraled out of control, which it eventually did.

 

But the spiraling never stopped.

 

Over the weekend, President Trump and others put enormous pressure on Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, and they ultimately relented. Nvidia’s board said it was confident that Huang’s reinstatement poses no national-security risk. Trump, however, gave myriad explanations for this decision. He said that the personal indiscretions weren’t relevant (“Sex sells, fellas”). And that Huang might have gone to work for China (“He’s got a little blood in him”).

 

Where does this leave Rubio?

 

Trump’s ends-justify-the-means China policy has surprised many people, and Nvidia and its AI-powering chips are central to it. Rubio is on the short-list of people often mentioned to lead the GOP in the post-Trump era. But if Rubio tried to intervene with regards to Huang because he felt the CEO posed a national-security risk, and Trump ultimately sided with Huang, what does that mean for Rubio?

 

Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. So far, it seems like the most outspoken lawmakers—Republicans and Democrats—share concerns about Huang and Trump’s involvement. Lawmakers could end up rallying behind Rubio, whether he wants them to or not.

 

At an event Monday to welcome Qatar’s leader, Rubio appeared briefly in front of reporters. One asked him, “Mr. Secretary, is Jensen Huang’s reinstatement a national-security risk? Are you concerned about that?”

 

Rubio waited for the question to finish, turned and walked away.

People and Policies I’m Watching

Trump’s Tuesday: In addition to policy meetings, the president will participate in the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardoning.

What I’m Following

Huang’s reinstatement sparks criticism from Congress. News of Huang getting his job back got a frosty reception on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers of both parties said the decision was wrong. Huang’s “behavior does not support reinstatement,” and doesn’t excuse him from testifying before Congress, said Sen. Pete Ricketts (R., Neb.), a member of the Senate Banking Committee.

 

Democrats begin looking into companies with ties to Trump’s son. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D., Md.), the incoming House Judiciary Committee chairman, sent letters to four firms seeking records of their relationships with 1789 Capital, in which Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. Raskin alleges that 1789 Capital might have had advanced knowledge of federal contracting decisions, which Trump Jr. and the company have denied.

 

The AI build-out is crowding out the rest of the economy. The massive artificial-intelligence build-out has become the major force behind U.S. economic growth. But many of the things AI is vacuuming up—chips and electricity, labor and money—are resources that other businesses also need.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• The Pentagon is in preliminary talks with General Motors and other manufacturers to help mass produce military drones.

 

• U.S. believes Iran could be behind a string of cyberattacks against commercial ships.

 

• A federal appeals court cleared the U.S. Army to detonate 9,500 pounds of toxic lead azide on Wednesday in Iowa.

 

• Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D., Calif.) said he would resign after the House Ethics Committee found “substantial evidence” that he committed sexual misconduct.

 

• Trump uses speech at the Justice Department to condemn California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s decision to commute the death sentences in the state.
